PullRequest.Title: fix: allow workbench origin for remote resources
PullRequest.Body:
Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/336527

Electron 43 migrated `vscode-remote-resource` from the deprecated `registerHttpProtocol()` API to `protocol.handle()` backed by `net.fetch()`. The new handler preserves the request method, headers, and body. This is intentional, it keeps HTTP behavior intact and allows Electron to relay untouched `net.fetch()` responses without copying the response body through JavaScript.

Unlike the old protocol API, `net.fetch()` applies normal CORS validation. The renderer correctly sends:

```text
Origin: vscode-file://vscode-app
Sec-Fetch-Mode: cors
```

The remote server did not authorize that origin in its response, so Chromium rejected the resource.

## NetLog evidence

The net log capture shows that the remote file was found and returned successfully:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: image/svg+xml
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000
Vary: Origin
```

The response was missing:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: vscode-file://vscode-app
```

Chromium then ended the request with `CORS_REQUEST` followed by `CANCELLED`, which surfaced as `net::ERR_FAILED`.

## Why WSL and Dev Containers failed

WSL and Dev Containers use a direct host-and-port connection:

```text
vscode-remote-resource
→ protocol.handle()
→ net.fetch()
→ forwarded loopback HTTP endpoint
```

SSH uses `vscode-managed-remote-resource`, which reads through main process IPC and the remote file service. It does not use the affected HTTP fetch path.

## Why this is different from previous regressions

Earlier fixes covered `vscode-managed-remote-resource`:

- #319834 registered the managed scheme as CORS capable.
- #335241 fixed managed workbench request identification and response handling.

Those fixes remain valid and explain why SSH continues to work. The direct `vscode-remote-resource` path did not have equivalent end-to-end coverage. The remote resource endpoint now authorizes the exact native workbench origin

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: vscode-file://vscode-app
Vary: Origin
```

Existing configured web endpoint origins remain supported. The fix does not use a wildcard and does not authorize `vscode-webview://` origins. Webviews use the HTTPS virtual resource pipeline and should not get direct access to token protected remote files.

## Test coverage

The new tests cover both sides of the failure:

1. A server test verifies that native workbench and configured web origins are allowed, while webview and arbitrary origins are rejected.
2. An Electron integration test loads a real SVG from `vscode-file://vscode-app` through `vscode-remote-resource` and verifies that the server receives the expected CORS headers.

Scenarios.Scenario: Native desktop workbench renders remote images, fonts, or other resources from a direct WSL/Dev Container authority.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Chromium resolves a vscode-remote-resource URL, the Electron protocol handler awaits net.fetch to the forwarded HTTP endpoint, the remote server validates the token and origin, and serveFile stats and potentially opens/streams the file before the renderer can use it. The diff changes CORS authorization but does not add a new critical-path boundary.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Electron net.fetch relays the custom-scheme request to the remote authority over HTTP.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One HTTP request per browser cache miss or revalidation for each effective resource URL; browser caching/coalescing remains authoritative.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same net.fetch call, method, headers, body, and bypassCustomProtocolHandlers option were inline in CodeApplication; this PR only extracts them into a helper.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The fetch response must arrive before the resource can render.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: The remote server stats the requested file and, unless an ETag revalidation returns 304, opens and streams it.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One stat per server request and one open/stream per non-304 successful request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same serveFile path and CacheControl.ETAG behavior ran before the diff.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Stat and file streaming are required before the HTTP response completes.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The number of distinct remote resource URLs requested by the rendered workbench content after browser caching and request coalescing.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Chromium/Electron controls concurrent resource fetches; the PR adds no Promise.all fan-out, queue, limiter, or retry and preserves one net.fetch per protocol request.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Built-in and installed extension resources retain public max-age caching; other files retain ETag revalidation. The added Access-Control-Allow-Origin and existing Vary: Origin do not alter cache policy, keys, or coalescing in this code.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the old inline handler and new helper are operation-for-operation equivalent, while the server change performs only bounded header selection before the unchanged serveFile call.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Resource counts and remote filesystem/network latency vary by workbench content and remote environment, but the diff does not increase their cardinality or scheduling.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression. Native-origin requests now short-circuit before the existing web-origin regular expression, and the required network and filesystem work is unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: VS Code for the Web or a configured web endpoint loads a remote resource through the remote extension host agent.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The existing HTTP request reaches the remote agent, token/path checks run, the configured-origin regular expression is evaluated, and serveFile stats and potentially streams the file. The response-header extraction does not move a new operation onto this path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: The server stats and conditionally streams the requested remote file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One stat per effective HTTP request, with one stream only for a successful non-304 response.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Before the diff, the same endpoint called the same serveFile function with the same ETag and extension-resource max-age policies.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The requested media cannot load until the file response is available.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Distinct remote resources requested by web content after HTTP cache reuse and ETag revalidation.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: HTTP/browser request concurrency is unchanged; origin matching remains one synchronous regular-expression test per request with an origin, and there is no added fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Positive browser caching and ETag behavior are unchanged. Vary: Origin and allowed configured-origin handling already existed before this PR; there is no application cache or negative-cache change.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: before/after comparison shows the existing origin matcher and filesystem path are preserved, with the helper adding only a native-origin equality short-circuit.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Actual resource counts vary by page and extensions, but no changed mechanism scales beyond constant header work per existing request.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable performance regression; boundary count, cache behavior, and concurrency are unchanged.

Scenarios.Scenario: Electron unit-test runner startup and the new remote-resource CORS integration test.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: On app readiness, the runner now awaits two local module imports and binds one loopback HTTP server before creating/loading the main test window. The single new test invokes IPC, creates one hidden BrowserWindow, loads one local fixture, and performs one loopback fetch before assertion.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dynamically imports two built JavaScript modules and loads the local HTML fixture for the integration test.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two imports once per Electron test-runner process; one fixture navigation when the single test runs.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The runner did not import these modules or load this fixture.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The imports complete before the test window starts; fixture loading is on only the new test's critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Binds one loopback HTTP listener and serves one SVG request from the hidden integration-test window.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One listener per runner process and one loopback request for the single added test.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No dedicated remote-resource loopback listener or request existed in this runner.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Listener setup is awaited once before tests; the one response is awaited by the new test.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One Electron runner process and one newly added test invocation, independent of production resource count or suite test count.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: A single listener is shared for the process, and the integration test issues one request. The server is closed after reporter draining in non-development runs; no burst or unbounded listener creation occurs.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The fixture request has no meaningful warm-cache path, but it executes once; production caches are not involved.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the awaited startup work and cleanup are explicit in the changed harness code.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Exact module-import and loopback-bind duration varies by platform, but the work is constant and bounded rather than scaling with the suite.
Scenarios.Verdict: The harness gains small constant startup work, but there is no realistic scaling mechanism or material performance regression warranting a finding.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all eight changed files and every diff page. Traced production remote-resource network/filesystem behavior, cache policy, origin-check cost, browser concurrency, and the Electron integration-test lifecycle. The PR preserves production boundary cardinality and scheduling; no actionable performance finding or qualifying regression-fix record was identified.
